e: Latin advocatus (one called to help), from ad + vocare (to call).
t: Called (vocare) to defend: like « un avocat ». To advocate = prôner.

e: French appréciable, from Late Latin appretiare (to set a price on), pretium (price).
t: Same as « appréciable »: big enough to put a price on.

m: Anxiety about the future; also understanding or arrest.
t: Same as « appréhension »: fear seizes you.
Same as « archaïque »: archaeology.

m: Occupation of a position of dominant power.
t: « Avoir de l’ascendant sur »: having climbed above.
Auto + nomos = making your own law.
« Avide »: an avid reader devours books.

e: Old Norse bón (prayer, request). A favour granted in answer to a prayer.
t: A prayer answered: remote work was a boon for her.

m: Showing great skill; to complete perfectly.
t: Summed up to perfection: a consummate professional.

e: Middle English derthe, from dear (costly): when things are scarce, they are dear.
t: Dear + th: scarce things become dear.

m: To treat with disrespect; to break down.
t: Same as « dégrader »: step down.
Frighten away: terror.

m: To distinguish; also to treat unfairly.
t: On the GRE, discriminating often = discerning taste.

m: To deprive of a right, especially voting.
f: priver du droit de vote, marginaliser
t: Franc = free: taking away a citizen’s franchise.
The heart taken out: « découragé » (cœur).

m: Difficult to find, catch or remember.
t: It plays (ludere) its way out of your grasp: « éluder ».

m: Regularly found in a particular area.
t: Same as « endémique »: corruption endemic to the system.

e: Old French enticier (to set on fire, provoke), Vulgar Latin intitiare, from titio (firebrand).
t: Like « attiser »: stoking a fire to lure someone in.
Straight from « fêter ».

m: New and inexperienced; a young bird.
e: From fledge (to grow feathers), Old English flycge (able to fly).
t: A baby bird just getting feathers: a fledgling start-up.

m: To struggle clumsily; to be in confusion.
e: Perhaps a blend of founder and blunder (16th c.).
t: Thrashing about in mud: « patauger ».

e: Scottish, imitative of the sound (18th c.).
t: Say it out loud: guff-AW! « S’esclaffer ».
Feet tied: « empêcher » comes from the same word.

m: Not allowing fluid (or influence) to pass through.
t: Same as « imperméable », your raincoat.
Never ceasing: « incessant ».
Not clement: « un temps peu clément ».
« Ingéniosité ». Funny twist: it comes from ingenuous (naive).
Iocus = jeu, joke: jovial and jokey.

e: Old French maladie, from malade, Latin male habitus (in bad condition).
t: Straight from « maladie ».
Metal you can shape with a hammer (malleus, maillet).

m: To wander aimlessly; follow a winding course.
e: Greek Maiandros, a famously winding river in Asia Minor.
t: « Les méandres » of the river Maeander.

m: Debatable; or of no practical relevance.
e: Old English mōt (assembly, meeting) where matters were debated.
t: A question debated at the moot (assembly). “A moot point” = « sans objet ».
Same as « morose ».
« Muet »: a muted response, muted colours.
Hardened (dur) against persuasion.
« Orné »: ornate Baroque churches.

m: To treat condescendingly; also to be a customer of.
t: Acting like a father to an adult: condescending.

e: From pith, Old English pitha (the essential core of a plant).
t: All core, no fluff: a pithy remark.

e: Probably imitative of heavy footsteps (16th c.).
t: The sound of heavy boots: plod, plod.

m: A person who advocates a theory.
t: Someone who proposes.

m: A state of uncertainty over what to do.
e: Origin uncertain (16th c.); perhaps from Latin quando (when?).
t: « Quand? » — not knowing what or when to do.

m: Unconventional and slightly disreputable, but attractive.
t: Riff-raff with charm: « un air canaille ».

m: To go back on a promise.
t: Like « renier »: you deny your own promise.
Making a resolution = showing resolve.

m: A short period of rest or relief.
t: Same as « répit ».
Strong as an oak: « robuste ».

m: Mocking in an indirect, unkind way.
t: A snide remark: a fake compliment with a sneer.
Not solid, but close: stolid = unmoving, impassive.

m: To prevent someone from accomplishing something.
e: Old Norse þvert (across). To put something across someone’s path.
t: Laying a log across the path: thwarted plans.
Same as « transitoire ».
